name: Anathoth
summary: Priestly town associated with Jeremiah’s family and land purchase; commonly identified with the village area of Anata northeast of Jerusalem.
historicalContext: Anathoth belongs to the Benjamin/Judah highland setting immediately before and during the Babylonian crisis.
archaeology: The general identification is strong in historical geography, but the exact ancient settlement footprint and Jeremiah’s field are not recoverable as named archaeological features.

confidence.explanation: The modern Anata area preserves the name and fits the textual geography, but the atlas does not claim a precisely excavated “house of Jeremiah.”

name: Valley of Hinnom
locationNote: The valley system south/west of ancient Jerusalem is secure; this coordinate is only a display anchor.
summary: Valley adjoining Jerusalem, central to Jeremiah’s denunciation of Topheth and later Gehenna traditions.
historicalContext: The valley forms part of Jerusalem’s Iron Age topography and helps orient Jeremiah’s judgment oracles.

confidence.explanation: The valley’s broad topographic identity is secure, but individual ritual loci within it are less certain.

name: Topheth
summary: Cultic place condemned by Jeremiah in the Valley of Ben Hinnom.
historicalContext: The biblical texts locate Topheth in the Hinnom valley complex, but do not give a recoverable modern coordinate.

confidence.explanation: The valley context is clear; the exact ritual site is not established sufficiently to justify a normal map pin.

name: Ketef Hinnom
summary: Jerusalem burial-cave complex where two small silver amulets preserving wording related to the priestly blessing were discovered.
historicalContext: The finds illuminate late Iron Age religious/textual culture near the end of the monarchy; they do not name Jeremiah, Josiah, or another biblical individual.
archaeology: The silver amulets are among the most important epigraphic finds from late pre-exilic Jerusalem.

confidence.explanation: The archaeological site and find context are established; historical interpretation is kept separate from biblical ownership claims.

name: Ramat Rahel
summary: Major administrative and elite complex south of Jerusalem with important late Iron Age, Babylonian, and Persian-period phases.
historicalContext: Ramat Rahel helps visualize continuity and administrative reorganization in Judah/Yehud across the Babylonian and Persian transitions.
archaeology: Excavations document monumental architecture, stamped storage systems, and long-term administrative significance. Identifying specific officials remains interpretive.

confidence.explanation: The site is secure; its administrative role is strongly supported, while person-specific identifications are avoided.

name: Riblah
aliases: Riblah in the land of Hamath
summary: Northern Syrian headquarters where the biblical narrative places Nebuchadnezzar during the final judgment on Zedekiah and Judean officials.
locationNote: Commonly identified near modern Ribleh on the Orontes corridor; exact ancient extent is imperfectly known.

confidence.explanation: The regional identification near Ribleh fits name and route geography; the exact camp/royal headquarters cannot be pinpointed.

name: Carchemish
summary: Major Euphrates city where Babylonian and Egyptian forces fought in 605 BCE, a crucial chronological anchor for the end of Judah’s independence.
archaeology: The site is securely identified on the Turkey–Syria border. The 605 BCE battle is independently situated in Babylonian chronicle evidence.

confidence.explanation: Carchemish is securely identified archaeologically and historically.

name: Hamath
summary: Major Syrian city/region on the Orontes corridor, useful for understanding Riblah and northward imperial routes.

confidence.explanation: Ancient Hamath is securely associated with modern Hama; biblical “land of Hamath” can denote a wider region.

name: Tahpanhes
summary: Eastern Nile Delta site associated with the Judean refugees and Jeremiah after Gedaliah’s assassination.
archaeology: Tell Defenneh is the standard candidate for Daphnae/Tahpanhes; exact identification details and specific “palace pavement” correlations require caution.

confidence.explanation: Tell Defenneh is the leading historical-geographic identification, but the atlas does not identify a particular excavated surface as Jeremiah’s action site.

name: Memphis (Noph)
summary: Ancient Egyptian capital region named Noph in Jeremiah; important context for Judean communities in Egypt.

confidence.explanation: Noph is securely identified with Memphis in standard historical geography.

name: Pathros / Upper Egypt
locationNote: Pathros is a regional designation for Upper Egypt; the coordinate is only a map label anchor.
summary: Regional name for Upper Egypt, included among places where Judeans are addressed in Jeremiah 44.

confidence.explanation: The general association with Upper Egypt is strong; no single city coordinate should represent the region.

name: Migdol in Jeremiah’s Egyptian setting
summary: An Egyptian place named with Tahpanhes, Noph, and Pathros in Jeremiah 44; multiple eastern-Delta sites named “Migdol/tower” complicate exact identification.

confidence.explanation: The textual region is Egyptian, but the exact Migdol intended is insufficiently secure for a pin.

name: Perath in Jeremiah 13
summary: Place/river term in Jeremiah’s linen-belt sign action. The Hebrew commonly denotes the Euphrates, but the extraordinary travel implied has generated alternative local proposals.

confidence.explanation: The lexical reading “Euphrates” is straightforward, while some interpreters propose a local site such as Parah. The atlas leaves the sign-action location unpinned.

interpretations.title: Euphrates reading
interpretations.summary: Hebrew perat ordinarily names the Euphrates; the narrative may intentionally emphasize a long symbolic journey.

interpretations.title: Local Parah proposal
interpretations.summary: Some interpreters have proposed Parah near Anathoth to avoid repeated Euphrates travel; this is not certain.

name: Neo-Babylonian Empire
locationNote: The point is a searchable label near Babylon, not an empire centroid or border claim.
summary: Mesopotamian empire under Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar II that defeated Egypt’s position in Syria-Palestine and conquered Judah.

confidence.explanation: The empire is historically established; the searchable point is only an anchor and changing imperial borders are rendered separately as generalized context.

name: Nebuchadnezzar II’s Southern Palace at Babylon
summary: Excavated Neo-Babylonian royal palace complex at Babylon, useful context for the court world imagined in Daniel.
archaeology: The palace complex is archaeological reality; the atlas does not label a specific hall as the scene of Daniel 5.

confidence.explanation: The palace complex is established; correlation with a particular biblical court scene is not archaeologically demonstrated.

name: Nippur
summary: Major Babylonian city and administrative landscape south-east of Babylon; important for locating exilic settlement evidence in central/southern Babylonia.

confidence.explanation: Ancient Nippur is securely identified archaeologically.

name: Kebar Canal
locationNote: Displayed in central Babylonia as an approximate area anchor. This is not an exact reconstructed canal course.
summary: Babylonian waterway beside which Ezekiel locates himself among the exiles.
historicalContext: The Kebar should not be confused with the Khabur River in northern Mesopotamia; scholarship commonly relates it to a Babylonian canal system.

confidence.explanation: The Babylonian canal context is strong, while the precise ancient watercourse cannot responsibly be drawn as a modern line from the biblical text alone.

name: Tel-abib in Babylonia
summary: Settlement by the Kebar where Ezekiel says he sat among the exiles. It is unrelated to the modern Israeli city Tel Aviv.

confidence.explanation: Its Babylonian setting by the Kebar is textual, but no secure archaeological coordinate is established.

name: Al-Yahudu (“Town of Judah”)
summary: Settlement known from cuneiform documents involving Judeans in Babylonia, important independent evidence for exile-community life.
historicalContext: The tablets document families, land tenure, obligations, and economic integration over generations.

confidence.explanation: Al-Yahudu is historically attested in tablets, but its exact archaeological location is not securely established and should not be pinned.

name: Judean Exile Settlement Zone in Babylonia
locationNote: Broad orientation anchor derived from textual/cuneiform evidence, not a bounded ethnic enclave.
summary: Generalized central/southern Babylonian landscape where Judean exiles are attested by biblical and cuneiform sources.

confidence.explanation: The broad Babylonian setting is strong; communities were dispersed and the point is only a search/display anchor.

name: Euphrates River
locationNote: Display point on the Babylonian reach; the river extends far beyond this coordinate.
summary: Major Mesopotamian river structuring imperial travel and settlement; named explicitly in Jeremiah and elsewhere.

confidence.explanation: The river is secure; this pin merely provides a map entry point.

name: Tigris River
locationNote: Display anchor only; Daniel 10 does not identify a specific modern point along the river.
summary: Major Mesopotamian river used as the setting of Daniel 10.

confidence.explanation: The Tigris is established; the exact visionary location along it is unspecified.

name: Plain of Dura
summary: Plain in the province of Babylon where Daniel 3 sets Nebuchadnezzar’s image. Numerous “Duru/Dura” place-names prevent a secure identification.

confidence.explanation: The literary setting is Babylonian, but no candidate is secure enough for a normal atlas pin.

name: Achaemenid Persian Empire
locationNote: Searchable label anchor near Persepolis, not an imperial capital claim for every reign or a substitute for changing borders.
summary: Empire founded by Cyrus II that conquered Babylon in 539 BCE and governed Judah/Yehud through the Persian period.

confidence.explanation: The empire is established; boundaries changed and are shown only as generalized time-aware context.

name: Susa
summary: Major Elamite and Achaemenid royal center; primary setting of Esther and a visionary setting in Daniel 8.
archaeology: The site and Achaemenid palace complex are securely known. The atlas does not identify a specific excavated room as Esther’s banquet hall.

confidence.explanation: Ancient Susa is securely identified.

name: Ulai Canal
locationNote: Anchored near Susa for orientation; the exact ancient channel alignment is not represented.
summary: Watercourse in Daniel 8’s Susa vision.

confidence.explanation: Association with the Susa hydraulic landscape/Eulaios is plausible, but exact ancient channel geometry is uncertain.

name: Ecbatana
summary: Median/Persian royal city called Achmetha in Ezra 6, where the narrative says Cyrus’s memorandum was found.
archaeology: The identification with Hamadan is standard, though ancient remains lie beneath/around the modern city and exact archive locations cannot be reconstructed.

confidence.explanation: Ecbatana is strongly associated with Hamadan; precise palace/archive geography is not recoverable.

name: Persepolis
summary: Monumental Achaemenid royal center founded under Darius I; not named in the Hebrew Bible but essential context for the Persian imperial world.
archaeology: Palaces, reliefs, administrative tablets, and inscriptions make Persepolis one of the best-documented Achaemenid centers.

confidence.explanation: The site is securely identified; it is included as historical context rather than a biblical event location.

name: Pasargadae
summary: Early Achaemenid royal center associated with Cyrus II, useful for understanding the Persian world behind Ezra.

confidence.explanation: Pasargadae is securely identified archaeologically; the Bible does not narrate an event there.

name: Elam / Susiana
locationNote: Broad geographic label; not a surveyed provincial border.
summary: Southwestern Iranian region containing Susa, named in Daniel 8’s literary setting.

confidence.explanation: The historical region is established, but territorial definitions changed and are generalized.

name: Yehud (Persian-period Judah)
locationNote: The pin is a searchable label at Jerusalem. Actual provincial extent varied and is shown only as generalized context.
summary: Small Persian-period province centered on Jerusalem, the political setting of much of Ezra and Nehemiah.
historicalContext: Yehud was part of the larger western Achaemenid administrative system, often discussed within the satrapy/province “Beyond the River.”

confidence.explanation: Yehud is historically well attested, but exact borders by decade are not recoverable as modern cadastral lines.

name: Beyond the River (Abar-Nahara)
locationNote: Broad searchable anchor in the Levant; administrative extent and terminology changed across Achaemenid rule.
summary: Western Persian administrative designation used in Ezra for the territory west of the Euphrates.

confidence.explanation: The administrative concept is established; the point and context polygon are schematic.

name: Ahava
summary: Gathering place where Ezra assembles the returning group before departure toward Jerusalem.

confidence.explanation: The textual role is clear, but no modern location is established. It is therefore omitted from route geometry as a fixed point.

name: Casiphia
summary: Place from which Ezra requests Levites and temple servants during the Ahava encampment.

confidence.explanation: Casiphia’s location is not securely identified and receives no normal map pin.

name: Elephantine
summary: Island on the Nile with a fifth-century BCE Judean/Jewish military community and temple documented in Aramaic papyri.
historicalContext: Elephantine demonstrates that Persian-period Judean/Jewish life extended well beyond Yehud and Babylonia.
archaeology: Papyri document community institutions and a temple to YHW. This historical context is not narrated in Ezra–Nehemiah.

confidence.explanation: The site and documentary archive are securely identified.

name: Early Second Temple footprint
summary: Temple completed in the reign of Darius I according to Ezra. Its broad location belongs on the Temple Mount, but the exact Persian-period architectural footprint is not independently recoverable.

confidence.explanation: The canonical and historical temple location belongs to Jerusalem’s Temple Mount tradition; a precise Persian-period plan should not be pinned as though excavated.

name: Nehemiah’s wall circuit
summary: Wall and gate system rebuilt in Nehemiah’s narrative. Archaeology illuminates Persian-period Jerusalem, but the exact line and identification of every named gate remain debated.

confidence.explanation: Jerusalem is secure, but the full fifth-century wall circuit cannot responsibly be rendered as one unquestioned polyline.

name: Cush / Nubia
locationNote: Broad regional label in the Nile valley south of Egypt; the coordinate is not a border or capital.
summary: Nile-valley region south of Egypt referenced in prophetic and Persian-imperial biblical geography.
historicalContext: The extent of Kushite/Nubian states changed through time. The atlas uses a broad orientation anchor only.

confidence.explanation: Cush/Nubia is a secure historical-geographic region, while exact biblical-era borders vary by century.

name: Thebes (No-Amon)
summary: Major Egyptian city invoked in Nahum as an example of a seemingly powerful city that had nevertheless fallen.
historicalContext: Nahum 3 compares Nineveh with No-Amon/Thebes; Assyria sacked Thebes in 663 BCE, providing the historical background for the comparison.

confidence.explanation: No-Amon is securely identified with Egyptian Thebes.

name: Teman in Edom
summary: Edomite place/region used in prophetic literature as a poetic-geographic representative of Edom.
historicalContext: Several southern Jordan/Edomite identifications have been proposed, but the exact site intended in every prophetic text is not secure.

confidence.explanation: The Edomite regional association is clear, but the atlas avoids selecting one archaeological site as definitive Teman.
